concepts.name: Approval and Continuation of National Emergency: Parliamentary Timelines
key_dimensions: Initial proclamation valid for 1 month without parliamentary approval (44th Amendment changed from 2 months)
Requires special majority (2/3rd members present & voting + majority of total membership) in EACH House within 1 month
Continues in 6-month intervals requiring fresh special majority approval each time
UPSC trap: Distinction between approval majority vs. revocation majority requirements

concepts.name: Lok Sabha's Exclusive Power to Revoke National Emergency
key_dimensions: Only Lok Sabha (not Rajya Sabha) can pass a resolution to revoke National Emergency by simple majority
Special sitting must be convened if 1/10th of total Lok Sabha members give written notice to the Speaker (or President if House not in session)
Rajya Sabha has no role in revocation — UPSC trap on asymmetry between approval and revocation
Contrast with approval which requires BOTH Houses

concepts.name: Role of Rajya Sabha During National Emergency: Asymmetric Powers
key_dimensions: Rajya Sabha approves but cannot revoke National Emergency — asymmetry is a high-yield UPSC trap
Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved; its continuous existence provides institutional check during Emergency
Rajya Sabha's legislative role expands as Parliament can legislate on State List subjects
No provision for Rajya Sabha to independently check executive overreach during Emergency

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List During National Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 250: Parliament gains power to legislate on State List subjects during National Emergency
Such laws cease to operate 6 months after Emergency ends (not immediately)
Centre can give directions to States on any matter (Article 353)
UPSC trap: Laws made under Article 250 do not become permanently valid; automatic expiry clause

concepts.name: Extension of Lok Sabha's Term During National Emergency
key_dimensions: Parliament can extend Lok Sabha's term by 1 year at a time (Article 83(2)) during National Emergency
Extension cannot go beyond 6 months after Emergency ceases
Rajya Sabha term is NOT extendable — members retire on schedule regardless of Emergency
UPSC trap: This is a legislative act, not a Presidential Order; requires ordinary majority

concepts.name: Presidential Rule (Article 356): Parliamentary Approval Mechanism
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within 2 months by simple majority (not special majority)
If Lok Sabha is dissolved and approval is pending, Rajya Sabha alone can approve — unique exception
Continues for 6 months at a time; beyond 1 year requires special conditions (National Emergency + Election Commission certification)
UPSC trap: Article 356 approval requires simple majority, unlike Article 352 which requires special majority

concepts.name: Rajya Sabha's Unique Approval Power During President's Rule When Lok Sabha is Dissolved
key_dimensions: Only instance where Rajya Sabha can singly approve a proclamation without Lok Sabha concurrence
Approval is provisional until newly constituted Lok Sabha approves within 30 days of its first sitting
This is a critical exception to bicameral requirement — high-yield UPSC trap
Contrast with National Emergency where no such Rajya Sabha-alone approval exists

concepts.name: Maximum Duration and Parliamentary Re-approval of President's Rule
key_dimensions: Normally cannot exceed 3 years total in a State
Beyond 1 year: requires both National Emergency in India/State AND Election Commission certifying elections cannot be held
Parliament must re-approve every 6 months — institutional check on executive overreach
UPSC trap: The 3-year maximum and the twin conditions for extension beyond 1 year

concepts.name: Parliamentary Control Over Financial Emergency (Article 360)
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within 2 months by simple majority
Unlike National Emergency, NO special majority required — UPSC trap
Once approved, continues indefinitely until revoked — no periodic re-approval required
Parliament's role limited to initial approval; President can give directions to States on financial matters

concepts.name: Comparison of Parliamentary Approval Majorities Across Three Types of Emergency
key_dimensions: National Emergency (Art. 352): Special majority (2/3rd present & voting + majority of total membership) in BOTH Houses
President's Rule (Art. 356): Simple majority in BOTH Houses (or Rajya Sabha alone if Lok Sabha dissolved)
Financial Emergency (Art. 360): Simple majority in BOTH Houses
UPSC trap: Only National Emergency requires special majority; other two require simple majority

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Parliamentary Approval of Emergency Proclamations
key_dimensions: Pre-44th Amendment: Courts had limited review power (Makhan Singh case)
Post-44th Amendment and S.R. Bommai (1994): Courts can examine whether Cabinet's advice existed and whether material facts justify proclamation
S.R. Bommai: Presidential satisfaction is not immune from judicial review; floor test preferred over Governor's report
Parliament's approval does not immunize Emergency from judicial scrutiny — separation of powers principle

concepts.name: 44th Amendment Act, 1978: Strengthening Parliamentary Oversight
key_dimensions: Changed approval period from 2 months to 1 month for National Emergency
Introduced written Cabinet recommendation requirement before President can proclaim Emergency
Introduced Lok Sabha revocation by simple majority on notice by 1/10th members
Changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' — raised the threshold for proclamation

concepts.name: Parliament's Delegated Legislative Power to Executive During Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 357: When Parliament legislates on State List during Art. 356, it can delegate powers to President
President can further sub-delegate to an authority he specifies
Such delegated laws continue for 6 months after proclamation ceases
UPSC trap: Article 357 delegation is specific to President's Rule, not National Emergency

concepts.name: Suspension of Fundamental Rights and Parliament's Role: Articles 358 vs 359
key_dimensions: Article 358: Automatic suspension of Article 19 rights during National Emergency (external aggression/war only, not armed rebellion) — no Parliamentary resolution needed
Article 359: President by Order (laid before Parliament) can suspend right to move courts for enforcement of specified FRs
Parliament must approve Article 359 Orders — active oversight role vs. passive role in Article 358
UPSC trap: Article 358 is automatic; Article 359 requires Presidential Order laid before Parliament

concepts.name: Parliament's Power to Reduce or Withhold State Grants During Financial Emergency
key_dimensions: President can direct reduction of salaries of all government servants including Supreme Court and High Court judges
All Money Bills of States require Presidential assent — Parliament's financial supremacy reinforced
Parliament does not need to pass specific legislation; President's directions are self-executing
UPSC trap: Judges' salaries can be reduced during Financial Emergency (exception to normal protection)

concepts.name: Parliamentary Sessions and Quorum Requirements During Emergency Oversight
key_dimensions: Special sitting for Lok Sabha revocation must be held within 14 days of notice by 1/10th members
Normal quorum rules (1/10th of House membership) apply during Emergency approval sessions
Parliament must be in session or a special session convened — President cannot indefinitely delay calling Parliament
UPSC trap: The 14-day window for special sitting is specific and frequently tested

concepts.name: Executive Ordinance-Making Power vs. Parliamentary Legislation During Emergency
key_dimensions: President can promulgate ordinances even during Emergency if Parliament is not in session (Article 123)
Ordinances must be approved by Parliament within 6 weeks of reassembly — oversight mechanism continues
Emergency does not suspend Parliament's power to review ordinances; institutional checks remain
UPSC trap: Emergency and ordinance-making are independent powers; Emergency doesn't enhance ordinance validity

concepts.name: State Legislature's Fate During Presidential Rule: Parliamentary Substitution
key_dimensions: Parliament assumes the legislative functions of State Legislature under Article 356
State Legislature is either suspended or dissolved — Parliament becomes surrogate legislature
Laws made by Parliament for the State continue even after President's Rule ends (unlike Article 250 laws)
UPSC trap: Permanency of laws made under Article 356 vs. auto-expiry of laws under Article 250

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law Applicability During Emergency Voting
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule applies to voting on Emergency approval/revocation resolutions
A member who votes against party whip on Emergency resolution can face disqualification
This creates tension between parliamentary oversight and party discipline — reduces independent legislative check
UPSC angle: Structural weakness in parliamentary oversight due to anti-defection provisions

concepts.name: Historical Instances of Parliamentary Oversight Failure: 1975 Emergency
key_dimensions: 39th Amendment placed President's election outside judicial review — Parliament complicit in undermining oversight
Lok Sabha extended its own term during 1975-77 Emergency using Article 83(2)
42nd Amendment (1976) curtailed judicial review and expanded executive power with parliamentary sanction
UPSC angle: Lessons leading to 44th Amendment as corrective institutional reform
